newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak premier plans talks on bank credit problems.
newsitem.headline: Slovak premier plans talks on bank credit problems.

text.p: Slovak Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar is planning to meet on Saturday with top central and commercial bankers to challenge them to improve credit conditions, his spokeswoman said on Monday.

"Mr. Premier has agreed with the National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) governor to meet along with commercial bankers to find the way out of the current situation," Meciar's spokeswoman Magda Pospisilova told Reuters.
She said the meeting, which Meciar alluded to in a radio address at the weekend, was "planned" for Saturday.
Meciar has criticised a recent surge in interbank interest rates, and hinted that a total overhaul of banking practices, especially with corporate clients, might be necessary.
"The credit restriction...stops everything, negative and positive," Meciar said in the address broadcast late on Friday.
"The government is very critically assessing this situation...we shall talk about these issues very sincerely and openly, and challenge banks to improve the situation."
The National Bank of Slovakia (NBS), the central bank, in early January moved to curb domestic lending by severely curtailing refinancing possibilities for local banks.
Since then, interbank money market rates have been volatile, rising to as much as 26 percent across all maturities but then dropping to 12 percent, in a very unbalanced market.
On Monday, rates were back up to between 15.5 percent for overnight money to 17.5 percent for six-month funds.
Meciar said in the address that the government would look to take some of the pressure off banks by speeding up the bankruptcy process, as few troubled enterprises have been shut.
He also said that the state must start more agressively reviewing cases where large share acquisitions have been leveraged with increasingly more expensive bank credit.

"The state must be essentially stricter because a funny situation is in Slovakia where...I take care of how to borrow today, and then you take care of how I will pay you back. This cannot last," Meciar said.
"There is too many debtors, and debt amounts are too high."

He said his cabinet is considering sanctions against those who are "buying up properties, transferring assets onto one company and liabilities onto another, while intending to keep the assets and leave the liabilities for banks and the state for bankruptcy".
Meciar did not specify what companies he meant.
"Let's start again, with new programmes, and a clean table," Meciar said.
Meciar said the government is currently completing new legislation on corporations and commerce and where one "goal" would be to releive old debts.

"Everyone will contribute to the indebtedness elimination... banks will do so, the government will do so, and according to our calculation, the maximum overall sum which may be at stake in such disburdening (of debt) is 75 billion crowns," Meciar said.
"We can solve this amount from the inside of the state --it is a huge economic power," he added.
-- Bratislava Newsroom, 42-7-563-3687
